chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Al-Husayn ibn Ishaq, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Ali ibn Fazzal, from Fazalat ibn Ayyub, all from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from Amr ibn Ikrama, who said:

I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'There is a neighbor of mine who bothers me.' He said, 'Be merciful to him.' I said, 'May Allah not have mercy on him.' So he turned his face away from me. I disliked leaving him, so I said, 'He does such and such to me, and keeps doing it and bothers me.' He said, 'What do you think, if I were to bring him into the open, would you be more just than him?' I said, 'Yes, I would exceed (in fairness) upon him.' He said, 'That one is from those who envy people for what Allah has given them of His grace. When he sees a blessing upon someone, if that person has a family, he makes his affliction upon them; and if he has no family, he makes it upon his servant. If he has no servant, he stays awake at night and is wrathful by day.'

A man from the Ansar came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'I bought a house among the clan of so-and-so, and the closest neighbor to me is one from whom I do not hope for goodness nor do I feel safe from his evil.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) commanded Ali (peace be upon him), Salman, Abu Dharr, and I forgot the other one, and I think it was Al-Miqdad, to call out in the Masjid with their highest voices that, 'There is no faith for the one whose neighbor is not safe from his deeds.' So they called it out three times.
Then he gestured with his hand to every forty houses from in front of him, from behind him, from his right, and from his left.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on difficult neighbors and how far does the right of a neighbor extend?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated through the chain of al-Kulayni, illustrates the practical application of neighborly rights by contrasting the Prophet’s directive to show mercy with the reality of enduring a neighbor's envy and harm. It establishes a specific geographical scope for these rights, extending to forty houses in each cardinal direction, a metric often cited in Shia jurisprudence for defining the 'neighbor' in legal contexts. The narrative underscores that true faith is incomplete without the security of one's neighbor from one's own mischief, linking spiritual integrity directly to social conduct.
